title: Sebastian is buying the Sembler waterfront for $2.5 million. Where the money comes from, and what is next.
seoTitle: Sebastian Buys Sembler Waterfront: Cost and Next Steps
description: Sebastian's council voted 5-0 to buy the 1.3-acre Sembler property on Indian River Drive for $2.5 million. How it is paid for and what the city plans there.
dek: After talks that go back to at least 2022, the city council said yes to the docks next to Fisherman's Landing. The price came in above the appraisals, so the vote needed a supermajority. Here is the deal in plain numbers, and what it means for the riverfront.
facebook: Ever wonder what happens to those docks next to Fisherman's Landing? Sebastian just voted 5-0 to buy the Sembler waterfront for $2.5 million. Here's where the money comes from, what grants pay back, and what the city plans to do with it.
keywords: Sebastian working waterfront Indian River Drive
Treasure Coast Shellfish Sebastian oyster farm

body.text: If you drive Indian River Drive in Sebastian, you know the spot. It is the stretch of docks right next to Fisherman's Landing, where the old fishing town still looks like a fishing town. This week the city council voted to buy it.

Sebastian Daily reported on Nov. 5 that the council unanimously approved, 5-0, a purchase and sale agreement for the Sembler property. The price is $2.5 million. Here is what that means, in plain numbers.

body.title: The short version
body.text: Sebastian is buying about 1.3 acres with docks at 1527 and 1528 Indian River Drive for $2.5 million. The city pays the full price at closing, then expects two grant reimbursements totaling about $1.29 million. The city manager said the net hit to general fund reserves should be minimal once that money comes back.
The property sits at 1527 and 1528 Indian River Drive, next to the city-owned Fisherman's Landing site. It runs from U.S. 1 to the Indian River Lagoon and includes a large pier and dock structure.

The site's tenant is Treasure Coast Shellfish, the county's only oyster farm, run by Nicolette Mariano. She spoke in favor of the purchase at the meeting and said dock access has been essential to her business.
Council members said the purchase supports commercial fishing and aquaculture, not new homes. Mayor Fred Jones said the goal is to preserve and eventually expand the working waterfront.
This is the part that matters to anyone who pays city taxes. According to Sebastian Daily, the money at closing comes from three places:

items: About $990,000 from selling the city's old public works compound.
$250,000 already budgeted in the Community Redevelopment Agency as a grant match.
Roughly $1.26 million from general fund reserves, to cover the rest at closing.

body.text: Then some of that money is supposed to come back. The city expects reimbursable grants of $1.041 million from the Florida Communities Trust and another $250,000. City Manager Brian Benton said that once those reimbursements arrive, the net impact on general fund reserves should be minimal.

Council Member Christopher Nunn called the package a "no-brainer" because so little unrestricted city money is at risk. Sebastian Daily's report does not mention any change to property taxes from this purchase.
Why the vote needed a supermajority

Two recent appraisals averaged about $2.1 million. The $2.5 million price is above that. Under the city charter, paying more than the appraisal average takes a supermajority of the council. All five members voted yes.

items: July 2022: The council debated buying the land and voted 4-1 to get a second appraisal. The property was listed at $2.9 million, and the city's first appraisal came in much lower, Hometown News reported.
2023: The city had offered $1.2 million. The council turned down a $2.5 million counteroffer.

February 2026: The council unanimously approved a grant agreement with the Florida Communities Trust for $1,041,000. At the time, the city's own share was set at $694,000, and the total was close to $1.7 million. Price and terms had not been negotiated yet.
This week: Negotiations settled at $2.5 million, and the council approved the deal 5-0.

body.text: The vote lets the city manager and the city attorney close the sale and sign the paperwork once the remaining documents are complete. After the city owns it, staff's first priority is keeping the oyster farm in place while looking at public access and other amenities.

Back in February, Hometown News reported that council members said the existing dock would stay if the city bought the property. Next door, the vacant Hurricane Harbor building at Fisherman's Landing, once Crab-E-Bill's fish market, is expected to be torn down eventually and replaced with a new building on the same footprint.

items: Read the full Sebastian Daily story and the February Hometown News report linked below. Together they show how the price and the funding changed.
Watch for the closing. Once the sale closes, the city's plans for public access will start taking shape.
Speak up. Mariano used the public comment time at this meeting. Any Sebastian resident can do the same at a city council meeting when plans for the site come up.
Keep an eye on the grant money. The plan depends on about $1.29 million in reimbursements coming back to the city. Those are fair questions to ask at budget time.

faq.q: What is the Sembler property in Sebastian?
faq.a: It is a roughly 1.3-acre waterfront parcel with docks at 1527 and 1528 Indian River Drive, next to Fisherman's Landing. It runs from U.S. 1 to the Indian River Lagoon and is home to Treasure Coast Shellfish, the county's only oyster farm.

faq.q: How much is Sebastian paying for the Sembler property?
faq.a: $2.5 million. Two recent appraisals averaged about $2.1 million, so the purchase needed a supermajority vote under the city charter. The council approved it 5-0.

faq.q: How is Sebastian paying for the Sembler waterfront?
faq.a: About $990,000 from the sale of the old public works compound, $250,000 from the Community Redevelopment Agency and roughly $1.26 million from general fund reserves. The city expects $1.041 million from the Florida Communities Trust and another $250,000 back in grant reimbursements.

faq.q: Will the Sembler purchase raise Sebastian property taxes?
faq.a: The news reports do not mention any property tax change. City Manager Brian Benton said the net impact on general fund reserves should be minimal once the grant reimbursements arrive.

faq.q: What will happen to the Sembler docks in Sebastian?
faq.a: Council members said the site will support commercial fishing and aquaculture, not residential development. Staff's first priority after closing is keeping the oyster farm in place while exploring public access and other amenities.
